catalog_quote: A root in Kaytetye has one prominence. The stress pattern in Kaytetye roots is conditioned to whether the word is consonant-initial (Turpin & Ross 2012: 26). If the word is consonant-initial, this prominence is always on the initial vowel (62). Kayte [ˈkai.tə] ‘Grub.’ If the word is vowel-initial, the second vowel is stressed. Aleke [aˈlə.kə] ‘Dog.’ If there is an initial long vowel, i.e. /ɐː/, the initial vowel is stressed. Aherre /ɐ:rə/ → [ˈaː.rə] ‘Kangaroo.’ Polysyllabic suffixes show the same stress pattern. For example, fieldworkers agree that in the word in (65), there is a prominence in both the noun root and the proprietive suffix. Alek-akake dog-PROP [aˈlə.kaˌka.kə] ‘Having a dog.’ ... sweep_summary: Kaytetye is not in the catalog. The single title-works with stress in the title, Turpin 2007 'Artfully hidden' (Musicology Australia 29: 93-108, doi 10.1080/08145857.2007.10416590), is a song-rhythm/text-setting study of the Akwelye song series, not a word-stress description; it is paywalled at Taylor & Francis with no open copy (Unpaywall is_oa=false, Semantic Scholar CLOSED with abstract elided, archive.org 0 hits, Sydney eScholarship 403; Low acquisition priority: the same authors' open AMP 2021 paper (held by the project) already states the stress rule the song analyses use. The best first-hand statement read in this search of works with stress in the title is Panther 2021 (PhD, Newcastle; held by the project) s.3.5.1 pp. 80-81 and s.5.4.1 p. 124: one prominence per root on the first consonant-initial syllable (C-initial words sigma-1, V-initial words sigma-2), initial-/ɐː/ roots excepted, polysyllabic suffixes as separate stress domains, no feet. Corroborated by Koch 1980 p. 266 rule (18), San & Turpin 2021 p. 2, Breen 2001 p. 55 (Arandic-wide) and Harvey et al. 2023 p. 39 (consensus tonic = first medial vowel). If Kaytetye is added to the catalog, Panther 2021 is the recommended deciding source and the system is onset-conditioned (not length-conditioned). all lookups were by direct API/URL probes.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable that has an onset consonant: initial syllable in consonant-initial words, second syllable in (short-)vowel-initial words; i.e. the first vowel following a consonant is stressed. Onset-sensitive fixed stress at the left edge of the prosodic word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Panther 2021 (s.6.3.3.1, ch.8; echoed by Harvey et al. 2023: 52): no secondary stress on monomorphemic roots and no evidence for metrical feet; additional prominences arise only because polysyllabic suffixes and second constituents of complex words (e.g. Alek-akake [aˈlə.kaˌka.kə], Associated Path auxiliaries) form their own prosodic words, each stressed on its first onsetful syllable. San & Turpin 2021 instead describe left-to-right trochaic footing from the first onsetful syllable. Koch 1997: 285 notes Arandic languages mostly lack the common Australian penultimate secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Roots with an initial long vowel /ɐː/ (e.g. aherre [ˈaːrə] 'kangaroo', historically from loss of a velar glide per Breen 2001: 55) take stress on the initial vowel (Panther 2021: 81, 123 fn.17). Word-final vowels cannot be stressed (San & Turpin 2021: 2). Initial and final vowels are variably dropped in colloquial speech, which does not move the stress off the first post-consonantal vowel. Clitics do not receive independent stress (Panther 2021 s.5.4.2).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the prosodic word = root or polysyllabic affix (Panther 2021: 82, 124); complex words contain several prosodic words each with its own stress. Statements are based on citation/elicited forms transcribed by fieldworkers plus the kPhon acoustic database (Panther's Table 37 counts stressed vs unstressed transcriptions of initial #ɐ vs #ɐː). Same rule stated independently by Koch 1980: 266 (rule 18: V -> stressed / #(V)C __), Koch 1997: 285, Breen 2001: 55 (Arandic-wide), San & Turpin 2021: 2, Harvey et al. 2023: 39.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Kaytetye proper (kayt1238; older spellings Kaititj (Koch 1980), Kaytej (Koch 1984/1990)). Breen 2001 p.55, Koch 1997 p.285 and Harvey et al. 2023 p.39 state the rule for the Arandic group as a whole (aran1266), of which Kaytetye is a member; Panther 2021, San & Turpin 2021 and Koch 1980 state it for Kaytetye specifically. Note Glottolog's list for kayt1238 includes Capell 1953 'Waramunga', which is a different language (Warumungu) and was not pursued.

new_statements.reading: Fixed, onset-conditioned stress: one prominence per root/prosodic word, on the first syllable that has an onset — initial syllable in consonant-initial words, second syllable in vowel-initial words; exception: roots beginning with long /ɐː/ stress the initial vowel. Polysyllabic suffixes are separate prosodic words with their own stress; no evidence for feet. Not a syllable-count-conditioned or weight-conditioned pattern (apart from the /ɐː/ exception), so for the catalog's length-conditioned scope this is an onset-conditioned system (consistent with the round-2 check's outside the catalog's scope ruling, records/). Independently corroborated by Koch 1980 p. 266 rule (18), San & Turpin 2021 p. 2, Breen 2001 p. 55 and Harvey et al. 2023 p. 39.

sources.quote: The stress rule, formalised in (18), assigns stress to the vowel that follows the first consonant position in a word. (18) V → stressed / # (V) C ___ This means that a word beginning with a consonant (cluster) is stressed on the first syllable, e.g. ... while vowel-initial words receive stress on the second syllable
sources.note: p.266: 'The stress rule, formalised in (18), assigns stress to the vowel that follows the first consonant position in a word. (18) V -> stressed / #(V)C __. sources.quote: Kaytetye has fixed stress, like many Australian languages. Unlike most Australian languages, however, Kaytetye has word-initial vowels. Stress assignment in Kaytetye is onset-sensitive and footing proceeds trochaically from left to right starting with the first syllable with an onset, e.g. a(ˈlə.kə) 'dog' vs. (ˈku.ɾə) 'girl'; word final vowels can not be stressed, e.g. *[ˈku.ɾɪmˈbə]. Thus, in Kaytetye, the word-initial onsetless syllable can never be stressed
sources.note: p.2: 'Kaytetye has fixed word stress which is invariably placed on the first syllable of a word with an onset'; 'Stress assignment in Kaytetye is onset-sensitive and footing proceeds trochaically from left to right starting with the first syllable with an onset, e.g. a(ˈlə.kə) 'dog' vs. (ˈku.ɾə) 'girl'; word final vowels can not be stressed'; the word-initial onsetless syllable can never be stressed.

sources.quote: The most widespread stress rule in Arandic, usually stated: main stress falls on the first vowel that follows a consonant, does not have a simple statement in terms of conventional syllables, but is: stress falls on the second syllable with VC(C) syllables.
sources.note: p.55 (Arandic-wide): 'The most widespread stress rule in Arandic, usually stated: main stress falls on the first vowel that follows a consonant.. is: stress falls on the second syllable with VC(C) syllables.' s.4.5 Kaytetye (pp.59-61) treats vowels/prepalatalisation only, no Kaytetye-specific stress rule.
